newsitem.title: UK: Nomura woes cast shadow over London JGB expansion.
newsitem.headline: Nomura woes cast shadow over London JGB expansion.

text.p: Nomura Securities's plans to expand trading in Japanese government bonds (JGBs) in London have been thrown off track by the widening scandal at the parent company in Japan, industry sources said on Tuesday.

Nomura Securities Co Ltd is under investigation in Japan for allegedly making illegal payments to racketeers. Since the scandal broke in March, Nomura's president and 15 board members have resigned, and the bank was suspended from JGB auctions and underwriting.
"Nomura in London was planning to build up the JGB business, and now it's a case of sitting around with long faces because there is no access to the primary market," said an industry source.

Earlier, the scandal appeared to be spreading as Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank's (DKB) premises were raided, amid unconfirmed reports that it offered questionable loans to racketeers at the heart of the Nomura debacle.

Sources said part of Nomura Securities's expansion plan at Nomura International in London involved Mark Cutis, who joined as managing director of the international markets division, leaving his position as treasurer of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
A spokesman for Nomura International declined to comment.
Traders said Nomura plays a relatively small part in the London JGB market, although it usually has a noticeable presence. That presence has dwindled in recent months, traders said.
But they said the company's absence is currently having only a minor impact, as non-domestic demand for JGBs is still at a low ebb, curbed by the low yields they offer.

"There isn't really a liquidity problem in London at the moment," said a JGB trader at a Japanese bank in London. "There's not much interest and the rest of the market can handle Nomura not being there."
The benchmark 182nd Japanese bond issue was yielding 2.48 percent by 1100 GMT.
However, an industry commentator, who declined to be identified, said Nomura's London activities were suffering, and the problem was likely to worsen.
"Although business is continuing, the flow of information out of Japan is not as good as it might be," the commentator said. "The secondary market offers fewer opportunities."

Nomura's share of underwriting 10-year JGBs was expected to be divided up among other brokerages in the JGB underwriting group. When the Japanese Ministry of Finance offers 10-year JGBs every month, 60 percent of the offered volume is sold through a price-competitive auction. The rest is sold through underwriters.
On Wednesday, the MoF will auction 10-year JGBs. The amount is likely to be 1.0 trillion yen, traders said.
Doug Jones, senior investment manager at Gartmore, the fund management arm of NatWest Investment Management, said volume of trade in JGBs was already light outside Japan.
"The main effect of this kind of thing is to make people careful about who they choose to deal with," he said. "I'm sure there are plenty more of these things to come."
